description: Owner-approved water-treatment claims (Stage 9.43). A numeric or efficacy treatment claim may appear in a member-facing file ONLY when a claim below matches it, in that file's own market. Nothing here may be copied between markets: an NZ figure has no AU entry and an AU figure has no NZ entry, so the gates fail closed on any crossing. Research and sources: admin-import/STAGE_9.42_OG09_WATER_TREATMENT_RESEARCH.md.

unavailableSources.title: enHealth guidance - The use of rainwater tanks
unavailableSources.authority: enHealth / Australian Centre for Disease Control
unavailableSources.note: The PDF would not download (three attempts, 2026-09-23). Owner ruling 3: do not cite, do not summarise, do not infer its contents, do not treat as supporting evidence. It may be reviewed and added if it becomes readable normally.

claims.allowedWording: Boil the water for one minute. Boiling is the simplest and most effective method to reliably kill Cryptosporidium parasites and other germs.
claims.authority: Health New Zealand - Te Whatu Ora; HealthEd HE10148; Building Performance, MBIE
limitations: A jug with an automatic cut-off may be used only while it is full, and must be allowed to switch off by itself (HE10148).
Cooled boiled water is best used within 24 hours (Health NZ).
No New Zealand source gives an altitude or elevation adjustment, so none may be written.
contaminationExclusions: chemicals and toxins - boiling will not make the water safe (Taumata Arowai)
heavy metals, algal toxins - no NZ household source supports boiling for these

claims.allowedWording: Add 5 drops of plain, unperfumed household bleach to 1 litre of water, or half a teaspoon to 10 litres. Stir and leave the water to stand for 30 minutes before drinking.
claims.numericValue: 5 drops per 1 L; 1/2 teaspoon per 10 L; 30 minutes standing time
claims.authority: Water Services Authority - Taumata Arowai; New Zealand Food Safety (MPI); HealthEd HE10148
claims.householdApplicability: household emergency treatment, when boiling is not possible
limitations: Plain, unscented bleach only: no perfume, colour, surfactants or other additives; 'thick', 'gel', 'foam' or 'cleaner' on the label means it is not suitable.
Bleach and purification tablets do not work on protozoa such as Giardia and Cryptosporidium, so boiled or bottled water is preferred.
This is a drinking-water dose. It is not the dish-rinsing dose (1/4 cup per 10 L) or the roof-cleaning dose, and those may never be shown as drinking-water doses.
contaminationExclusions: any water under a Do Not Drink or Do Not Use notice

claims.allowedWording: Fill clean containers with tap water, add five drops of plain, unscented household bleach per litre, and do not drink it for at least 30 minutes.
claims.householdApplicability: household, preparing stored water before an emergency
limitations: This is a storage preparation method for tap water, not a treatment for water of unknown quality.
Collected rainwater must be disinfected before drinking; if you are uncertain about the quality of water, do not drink it.
contaminationExclusions: any water under a drinking water notice

claims.allowedWording: Do not assume a household water filter makes water safe. Most filters only remove one or two types of impurity, and filters can become contaminated - ask the supplier what the device can and cannot do.
claims.authority: Health New Zealand - Te Whatu Ora; HealthEd HE10148
limitations: No New Zealand source publishes micron ratings, pore sizes or removal percentages for household filters, so none may appear in an NZ file.
contaminationExclusions: microbiologically unsafe water - no NZ source supports a filter making it safe

claims.allowedWording: For a rainwater system used for drinking, MBIE lists the options as adding chlorine, using a very fine in-line filter or purifier, boiling the water for one minute, and ultraviolet light treatment.
claims.householdApplicability: household rainwater supply used for drinking
limitations: MBIE names the options only. It publishes no rating, pore size, UV dose, chlorine ratio or performance figure, and none may be added.
Ruling 10: NZ may state that UV is a treatment option and nothing more.
contaminationExclusions: anything under a drinking water notice

claims.allowedWording: You should have drinking water tested annually, and some councils also require periodic testing.
limitations: A test is a snapshot of one sample, not a treatment.

claims.allowedWording: Tanks should be inspected annually and cleaned if necessary; ideally tank cleaning is carried out by tank cleaning contractors.
limitations: Entering a tank needs ventilation and a second person present (HE10148).

claims.allowedWording: If harmful chemicals or toxins could be in the water, boiling will not make it safe - use bottled or tankered water and follow the advice of your supplier or public health unit. If you are uncertain about the quality of the water, do not drink it.
claims.authority: Water Services Authority - Taumata Arowai; NEMA - Get Ready; HealthEd HE10148
limitations: Ruling 6: where no verified household treatment method exists for a contaminant, the member is directed to official or public-health advice and no treatment pathway is invented.

claims.allowedWording: Water used for drinking or food preparation should be brought to a rolling boil to make it safe. Kettles with automatic shut off switches can do this. Water should then be allowed to cool and stored in a clean container with a lid and refrigerated.
claims.householdApplicability: household, during a boil water alert
limitations: NSW publishes no duration for a rolling boil. NSW guidance is state guidance and may not be presented as a national Australian rule.

claims.allowedWording: Vigorous boiling for at least 1 minute will kill any disease-causing micro-organism present in the water.
claims.sourceDate: read live 2026-09-23 (no date shown on page)
limitations: WA guidance is state guidance. It may not be presented as a national Australian rule, and the New Zealand 'one minute' wording may not be substituted for it.
No Australian source read gives an altitude or elevation adjustment.

claims.allowedWording: NSW Health advises 2 drops of unscented 4-5% bleach per litre, or 4 drops if the water is cloudy, left to stand 30 minutes, and longer in colder water.
claims.numericValue: 2 drops per litre (4-5% available chlorine); 4 drops if cloudy; 30 minutes at 25C, 1 hour at 15C, 2 hours at 5C
claims.householdApplicability: household, when boiling is not possible during a boil water alert
limitations: The dose depends on the bleach strength and the contact time depends on water temperature.
It must carry its NSW attribution: it is not a national Australian ratio, and it may not appear in an NZ file.

claims.allowedWording: WA Health gives doses by strength: 10 drops per litre for 1% available chlorine, 2 drops for 4-6%, and 1 drop for 7-10%, left to stand 30 minutes.
limitations: Bleach must contain chlorine and no added perfumes or detergents.
WA attribution is required: it is not a national Australian ratio, and it may not appear in an NZ file.

claims.allowedWording: NSW Health notes that polypropylene and ceramic cartridge filters remove sediment and bacteria but will not remove viruses; activated carbon filters reduce chemicals, tastes, odours and colour but will not remove bacteria or viruses; micro/ultrafiltration membranes (0.1-0.01 micron) remove sediment and bacteria, and ultrafiltration may also remove viruses; reverse osmosis (0.001 micron) removes microorganisms and most residual chemicals.
claims.numericValue: 0.1-0.01 micron (micro/ultrafiltration); 0.001 micron (reverse osmosis); 30 micron and 5 micron pre-filtration
claims.householdApplicability: household rainwater and private supplies, with professional design advice
limitations: Micron values are NSW guidance and may appear only with that attribution. They may never appear in an NZ file (no NZ source publishes them).
'Not all filters remove harmful microorganisms' - a filter may not be described as making unsafe water safe.
contaminationExclusions: chemicals not covered by the filter type
viruses for ceramic and carbon filters

claims.allowedWording: WA Health says filters should not be relied upon to disinfect water, and that only a reverse osmosis system will effectively remove harmful bacteria.
match: \bWA\b[\s\S]{0,200}\bshould not be relied upon to disinfect\b
limitations: State guidance; not a national Australian rule.

claims.allowedWording: If a filter is being used for health reasons, look for the WaterMark or Plumbing Safety Type Test Mark and certification to AS/NZS 4348 or ANSI/NSF 53, and ask the supplier for the contaminant-removal claims and data.
claims.authority: NSW Health; WA Department of Health
limitations: A certification is a performance standard, not a guarantee that a given water source is safe.

claims.allowedWording: NSW Health advises that UV disinfection is effective against most bacteria, viruses and protozoa; that UV systems are most effective when the water is clear and free of particles, so rainwater may need to be filtered first; that UV does not remove chemicals; that UV systems require a power supply; and that water disinfected using UV should be used straight away, not stored in tanks.
limitations: Clear water and pre-filtration are required; UV leaves no residual disinfectant; constant power and lamp and sleeve maintenance are required.
State guidance: it may not be generalised to a national Australian requirement, and it may not appear in an NZ file.
contaminationExclusions: turbid or particle-laden water without pre-filtration

claims.allowedWording: WA Health says UV light is normally effective against all viruses, bacteria and protozoa, but that some low power UV systems cannot penetrate Cryptosporidium and Giardia; that water should be filtered before UV; that lamps and sleeves need regular replacement and cleaning; and that UV requires a continuous power supply and leaves no residual disinfectant.
limitations: State guidance; not a national Australian rule.

claims.allowedWording: A UV unit should carry the WaterMark or Plumbing Safety Type Test Mark and at least one of ANSI/NSF Standard 55 Class A systems (40 mJ/cm2), AS/NZS 3497 or AS/NZS 4348.
limitations: 40 mJ/cm2 is part of the name of the standard's Class A rating. It may never be written as 'the UV dose you need', and no other UV dose value may be written in either market.

claims.allowedWording: NSW Health's monitoring frequencies are for private water supply operators: microbiological testing monthly, chemical and physical testing annually, and free chlorine testing at least weekly where the supply is chlorinated.
claims.numericValue: monthly (microbiological); annually (chemical and physical); at least weekly (chlorine residual)
claims.householdApplicability: NOT household guidance - private water supply operators. It may be shown only with that label (ruling 11).
limitations: No Australian source read publishes a household testing frequency. An operator schedule may never be presented as a household requirement.

claims.allowedWording: Boiling and disinfection do not remove chemicals, blue-green algae toxins or metals. If chemical contamination or an algal bloom is suspected, the water is unsuitable for drinking - use an alternative supply and follow the advice of your state or territory health department. The Australian Drinking Water Guidelines say surface water or shallow groundwater should not be used as a source of drinking water without treatment, and NSW Health advises that water from dams, streams and rivers is not recommended as a source of drinking water unless it is filtered and disinfected.
match: \bnot recommended as a source of drinking water\b
\bshould not be used as a source of drinking water without treatment\b
limitations: Ruling 6: where no verified household treatment method exists for a contaminant, direct the member to official or public-health advice; do not invent a treatment pathway.

claims.allowedWording: The Australian Drinking Water Guidelines say the emphasis should be on selecting the best quality source water available, and that surface water or shallow groundwater should not be used as a source of drinking water without treatment.
match: \bshould not be used as a source of drinking water without treatment\b
limitations: This is the only national Australian statement relied on; every other Australian claim here is state guidance.
